extracted.intended_audience: poets and creative writers composing epistolary verse (readers of Horace/Ovid models)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for composing letters in verse (epistolary poetry), distinguishing Ovidian (amorous, tender) and Horatian (familiar, moral, satirical) manners and guidance on tone, imagery, versification, and authorial persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two classes of epistolary poetry (Ovidian vs Horatian)
rubrics_metrics.description: "These may be reduced into two _Classes_: In the one I shall range Love-Letters, Letters of Friendship, and Letters upon mournful Occasions: In the other I shall place such Epistles in Verse, as may properly be called Familiar, Critical, and Moral; to which may be added Letters of Mirth and Humour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the taxonomy to choose approach and tone: Ovidian for tender, passionate, love/mourning subjects; Horatian for familiar, critical, moral, humorous pieces. The passage implicitly advises matching subject-matter to the appropriate subgenre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ovidian manner: delicacy and tenderness of sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: "He that is ambitious of succeeding in the _Ovidian_ way, should first examine his Heart well, and feel whether his Passions (especially those of the gentler Kind) play easie, since it is not his Wit, but the Delicacy and Tenderness of his Sentiments, that will affect his Readers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize genuine, delicate feeling over cleverness; ensure the poet's emotions suit the softer, more languishing tone of Ovidian love-letters or mournful epistles. Versification should be 'soft' and numbers 'flowing and querulous.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Horatian manner: robust sense and worldly understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Qualifications requisite for writing Epistles, after the Model given us by _Horace_, are of a quite different Nature. He that would excel in this kind must have a good Fund of strong Masculine Sense: To this there must be joined a thorough Knowledge of Mankind, together with an Insight into the Business, and the prevailing Humours of the Age."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Horatian epistles cultivate strong practical judgment, knowledge of human nature, topical awareness, and moral sensibility. The author should be able to reflect on 'bright and dark sides of human Life' and write instructively rather than merely feeling-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horatian manner: wit, raillery, and conversational images
rubrics_metrics.description: "He must be a Master of refined Raillery, and understand the Delicacies, as well as the Absurdities of Conversation. He must have a lively Turn of Wit, with an easie and concise manner of Expression; Every thing he says, must be in a free and disengaged manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ refined mockery and subtle criticism; draw illustrations and images from common life; keep expression concise, easy, and conversational—avoid pedantry. Use humor and raillery judiciously to enliven moral or critical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw imagery and examples from common life
rubrics_metrics.description: "His Illustrations, his Comparisons, and the greatest part of his Images must be drawn from common Life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer quotidian, recognizable images over rarefied classical conceits to give epistles relatable force and ornament; this is especially stressed for Horatian-style letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the air of a recluse; appear a man of the world
rubrics_metrics.description: "He must be guilty of nothing that betrays the Air of a Recluse, but appear a Man of the World throughout."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an engaged, worldly persona in the voice of the epistle; avoid markers that make the speaker seem isolated from social life or unaware of contemporary manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain versecraft—avoid lapsing into prose or vulgar diction
rubrics_metrics.description: "...though never so familiar, still remember that he writes in Verse, and must for that reason have a more than ordinary care not to fall into Prose, and a vulgar Diction, excepting where the Nature and Humour of the Thing does necessarily require it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in conversational epistles attend to meter, cadence, elevated diction appropriate to verse; lapse into plain prose-like phrasing only when it serves comic or humoral effect. The warning is specifically aimed at preserving poetic form and elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care for versification and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: "His Versification likewise should be soft, and all his Numbers flowing and querulous." and the remark that "Horace hath been thought by some Criticks to be sometimes careless, as well as too negligent of his Versification; of which he seems to have been sensible himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to metrical smoothness, rhythmic flow, and musicality of lines. Negligence in versification undermines the quality of epistolary verse and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire, criticism, and panegyric—judicious and incidental
rubrics_metrics.description: "Strokes of Satyr and Criticism, as well as Panegyrick, judiciously thrown in (and as it were by the by) give a wonderful Life and Ornament to Compositions of this kind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce praise or satirical remarks sparingly and casually within the letter's conversational flow; they should feel incidental, not didactic or forced, to enliven the piece without breaking tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject dignity with epistolary tone (recollect into letter style)
rubrics_metrics.description: On treating sublime subjects: "The Poet surprizes us with his Pomp... He appears like the Visit of a King Incognito, with a mixture of Familiarity, and Grandeur... when the Dignity of the Subject hurries the Poet into Descriptions and Sentiments, seemingly unpremeditated, by a sort of Inspiration; it is usual for him to recollect himself, and fall back gracefully into the natural Stile of a Letter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a grand subject tempts overly pompous description, restore the intimate epistolary voice—blend familiarity with dignity so the piece reads as a letter that can briefly swell into grandeur but returns to conversational address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and restraint over implausible amplification (avoid false sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: In contrast to 'Exploded Fancies' the writer is told: 'Content to paint him, nor presume to praise; Their Charms, if Charms they have, the Truth supplies' and criticism of poets who 'debased Alcides, and dethron'd the Gods' with implausible fancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grandiose, unbelievable mythic or fantastical embellishments used merely to magnify the subject; honest, credible detail and truthful depiction provide persuasive charm and are preferable to extravagant hyperbole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware excessive obscurity—lines that are 'riddles' demand re-reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on a translated poem: 'Every Line in it is a Riddle, and the Reader must be forced to consider it twice or thrice, before he will know that the _Cynick's_ Tenement is a _Tub_, and _Bacchus_ his Cast-coat a _Hogs-head_, &c.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While complexity can be artful, be cautious of cryptic phrasing that makes lines puzzles; unnecessary obscurity hinders reader engagement—use obliqueness only with purpose and sparing frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial qualification: talent must match chosen manner
rubrics_metrics.description: "All I have to add is, that both these Manners of Writing may be made as entertaining, in their Way, as any other Species of Poetry, if undertaken by Persons duly qualify'd; and the latter sort may be managed so as to become in a peculiar manner Instructive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a mode (Ovidian or Horatian) consistent with the writer's strengths—emotional delicacy or worldly judgment—and ensure the author's abilities and knowledge suit the mode chosen; lacking qualification, the form will not succeed.
